source_text: eos iussionis terrore perculsos non erubuisse praevaricationis crimen admittere, ut contra priorem sententiam suam, qua gestis catholico dogmati affuerant, postea pronuntiarent malam hominum esse naturam
pass_a_gloss: that they, struck by terror of an order, were not ashamed to admit the crime of prevarication, so that contrary to their prior sentence, by which in the acts they had stood with catholic teaching, they afterward pronounced that the nature of human beings is evil

lemmas.lexica: LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself

pass_b_english: The Roman clergy were so frightened by an order that they were not ashamed to commit the crime of betrayal. In their earlier judgment, their recorded proceedings had supported catholic teaching; afterward, contrary to that judgment, they declared that human nature is evil.

choices.why: Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.
Julian claims the catholic faith against Augustine; keep lowercase-c catholic as the universal church, not a later confessional brand.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded. Julian is not first-English.

speaker: Julian and fellow bishops (Collective letter to Thessalonica, words preserved in Augustine, Contra duas epistolas Pelagianorum 2–4); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
